overview:
On the flat, hot alluvial plain where the Tigris and Euphrates run down to the Persian Gulf, a cluster of cities emerged in the fourth and third millennia BCE that between them invented much of what later peoples would take for granted. Uruk came first and was for a time the largest settlement on earth, with tens of thousands of inhabitants living around monumental mud-brick temple precincts. Ur, Lagash, Nippur, Eridu, Umma, Kish and a dozen others followed, each with its own patron deity, its own irrigation canals cut from the rivers, and its own ruler who governed in the god's name. The land had no timber, no stone and no metal, but it had grain, and the surplus from irrigated barley fields paid for everything else — copper from Anatolia and Oman, lapis lazuli from Afghanistan, carnelian from the Indus. Accounting for that surplus is the likeliest reason writing appeared here around 3300–3100 BCE: pictographic tokens pressed into clay, hardening over centuries into the wedge-shaped cuneiform script that would be borrowed by Akkadians, Hittites, Elamites and Persians for the next three thousand years.

The Early Dynastic period, roughly 2900 to 2334 BCE, is the era of the independent Sumerian city-state, and it was not a peaceful one. Rulers such as Eannatum of Lagash fought long wars with neighbouring Umma over border fields and water rights, disputes recorded on monuments like the Stele of the Vultures that are among the earliest surviving accounts of a specific historical quarrel. Around 2334 BCE Sargon of Akkad, a Semitic-speaking king from the north, conquered the whole plain and welded the cities into the first empire in the region; when Akkadian power broke apart, a Sumerian revival followed under the Third Dynasty of Ur, founded by Ur-Namma around 2112 BCE. His son Shulgi built a bureaucracy of extraordinary reach, standardising weights, measures, the calendar and the year-names, and leaving behind tens of thousands of administrative tablets — one of the densest archives from any ancient state. It lasted about a century. Amorite pastoralists disrupted the supply lines, harvests failed, and around 2004 BCE Elamite forces sacked Ur and carried its last king, Ibbi-Sin, into exile.

What followed was less an ending than a dissolution. The cities survived and in some cases prospered under the rival Amorite kingdoms of Isin and Larsa and, later, under Babylon, but the political label "Sumer" ceased to describe anyone's state. Sumerian itself, a language with no known relatives, had probably already stopped being spoken in ordinary households by around 2000 BCE, giving way to Akkadian. It did not disappear: scribes went on learning it as the language of liturgy, literature and scholarship for another two thousand years, copying hymns, laments and the poems about Gilgamesh long after nobody's mother tongue it was. Salinisation of the over-irrigated southern fields, meanwhile, gradually eroded the agricultural base that had made the whole thing possible, and the centre of Mesopotamian gravity shifted permanently north.
significance: Almost every element of the administrative state was assembled here first or close to first: writing, the sealed contract, the accounting archive, standardised measures, codified law, the professional scribe, the temple as landholder and employer, and the walled city itself as a political unit. Sumerian cuneiform became the writing system of the entire ancient Near East, and Sumerian literature — the flood story, the descent of Inanna, the Gilgamesh cycle — supplied narrative material that travelled into Akkadian, Babylonian and, by disputed but plausible routes, into the Hebrew Bible. The recovery of these texts in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries pushed the horizon of documented human history back by well over a thousand years and gave scholars their only direct evidence of how the first cities actually ran, in the words of the people running them.
coverage: This dataset holds no events at all beneath Sumer, so nothing here can be shown on the map — the overview is written from general reference works rather than from anything the map itself can plot. The surviving record is also badly uneven: it is overwhelmingly the paperwork of temples and palaces, so we know grain rations and canal maintenance far better than we know ordinary households, women's lives or rural settlement; the Sumerian King List mixes real rulers with legendary ones and cannot be read as chronology; the absolute dates before Ur III are contested by decades or more; the origins of the Sumerians and their language remain genuinely unresolved; and many southern Iraqi sites are unexcavated or have been damaged by looting and war.
